He is not striving for acceptance; he is walking in acceptance that is already complete. He is not fearing the future; he is walking toward a glory that has been guaranteed.

This produces a certain kind of believer:

  • Unhurried — because no opportunity can be lost when our times are in the Father's hand.
  • Unanxious — because no threat can separate us from the Father's love.
  • Unintimidated — because if God is for us, who can be against us?
  • Unbound — because we have no debt to the flesh and no fear of death.
  • Sustained in suffering — because the present is not worthy to be compared with the coming glory.
  • Free in service — because we serve from love, not from need.
  • Generous — because all things are ours in Christ, and we have nothing to lose.

This is the practical fruit of Romans 8: the free, confident, Spirit-empowered walk of the child of the Father.

8. THE BELIEVER'S CONTRIBUTION: KEEP YIELDING, KEEP RECKONING, KEEP PRESENTING

If we ask what the believer's responsibility actually is in light of all the Spirit does, the answer is consistent:

  • Reckon (Rom 6:11) — keep agreeing with the truth of who you are in Christ.
  • Present (Rom 6:13; 12:1) — keep yielding your members and your whole being to God.
  • Put to death by the Spirit (Rom 8:13) — keep refusing the deeds of the body.
  • Walk by the Spirit (Gal 5:16) — keep depending on the Spirit's leading.
  • Be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18) — keep being filled, an ongoing reality.
  • Set the mind on things above (Col 3:2) — keep your φρόνημα Spirit-oriented.

These are not earning. These are the believer's faithful response to the Spirit's empowering presence. The Spirit does His work in those who yield, reckon, present, and depend.

CROSS-WITNESSES — THE PATTERN ELSEWHERE

The Romans 8 pattern of life in the Spirit is confirmed throughout the NT.

Galatians 5:16-25 — The Walk by the Spirit

1599 Geneva:

"Then I say, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary one to another..."

The same theme: the believer walks by the Spirit, and in doing so, does not fulfill the lust of the flesh. The Spirit and the flesh are in opposition; the believer's deliverance is in walking by the Spirit.

Ephesians 3:16 — Strengthened by His Spirit in the Inner Man

1599 Geneva:

"That he might grant you according to the riches of his glory, that ye may be strengthened by his Spirit in the inner man,"

The Spirit strengthens the inner man — the regenerated core of the believer's being — with the Father's mighty power. This is the practical mechanism of Spirit-empowered living.

Ephesians 5:18 — Be Filled With the Spirit

1599 Geneva:

"And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess: but be fulfilled (filled) with the Spirit,"

The verb πληροῦσθε is present passive — "keep on being filled." This is not a one-time experience; it is an ongoing yielding to the Spirit's filling. The contrast with drunkenness is telling: as wine fills and controls a drunken person, the Spirit fills and controls the yielded believer — but unto life, not destruction.

Philippians 2:12-13 — Working Out and God Working In

1599 Geneva:

"...so make an end of your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you, both the will and the deed, even of his good pleasure."

The perfect statement of the cooperative relationship. The believer works out — kατεργάζεσθε — what is already true. God works in — ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν — both the willing and the working. The believer's effort and God's empowering are not opposed; they are integrated. The believer's responsibility is to work out what God works in.

A CLOSING SYNTHESIS — THE WHOLE PATTERN OF LIFE IN THE SPIRIT

Let me bring all the threads together.

The Architecture of the Spirit-Filled Life

StageRealityBeliever's Response
PositionIn Christ Jesus, no condemnation (Rom 8:1)Reckon yourself accepted in the Beloved
IndwellingThe Spirit dwells in you (Rom 8:9)Welcome and yield to His presence
IdentificationYou are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit (Rom 8:9)Walk according to this new orientation
MortificationThe Spirit empowers (Rom 8:13)Put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit
LeadingThe Spirit leads (Rom 8:14)Follow His leading; do not quench Him
Witness of SonshipThe Spirit bears witness (Rom 8:16)Rest in the confidence of sonship
Help in WeaknessThe Spirit intercedes (Rom 8:26)Pray in dependence; trust His intercession
Father's PurposeAll things work for good (Rom 8:28)Trust the Father's sovereign design
SecurityNothing separates from God's love (Rom 8:38-39)Walk boldly, freely, faithfully
FillingBe filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18)Keep yielding; keep being filled
Working outGod works in (Phil 2:13)Work out what He works in

The Vital Connection: Indicative → Spirit's Power → Believer's Response

Romans 6 gave us indicative → reckon → act.

Romans 8 adds the missing element: the Spirit's empowering presence as the means by which the believer's responsive action actually succeeds.

The full pattern is now:

  1. The indicative reality (what is true in Christ).
  2. The indwelling Spirit (the Father's gift, given through the Son).
  3. The believer's reckoning (agreeing with the indicative).
  4. The believer's yielding/walking/presenting (responsive action).
  5. The Spirit's empowering work (producing what the believer cannot produce by himself).
  6. The fruit of the Spirit (life, peace, conformity to Christ — the evidence).

This is the normal Christian life. Not flawless. Not effortless. Not without struggle. But empowered by the Spirit, oriented toward the Father, conformed progressively to the Son, secure in the Father's unbreakable love.

A FINAL OBSERVATION — THE GLORY OF THIS PATTERN

Brother, what we have surveyed in Romans 8 is the heart of Christian experience as the Apostle Paul taught it. The indwelling Spirit — whom we examined in Parts E and F as the Father's own essential being, poured out through the glorified Son — is not a static doctrine. He is the present, empowering, transforming, witnessing, interceding, comforting Companion of every believer.

The modern believer who walks in this reality is:

  • Free from the bondage of self-effort.
  • Free from the despair of Romans 7.
  • Free from the fear of separation.
  • Free from condemnation.
  • Empowered for victory over the flesh.
  • Led into the Father's purposes.
  • Comforted in suffering.
  • Strengthened in weakness.
  • Conformed progressively to the Son.
  • Secure forever in the love of God in Christ Jesus.

This is the inheritance of every child of God. This is what the Father has freely given us. This is what the Beloved Son purchased and made possible. This is what the Spirit applies and sustains.

Walk in the Spirit. Reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God. Yield to the Spirit's leading. Trust the Father's purpose. Rest in the unbreakable love that holds you. Look toward the coming glory.

This is life in the Spirit.

A QUESTION FOR YOU

Where would you have us go next?

(A) Continue with Romans 12 — the bodily presentation as a living sacrifice, the renewal of the mind, the practical outworking of life in the Spirit in community?

(B) Examine Galatians 5 in more depth — the walk by the Spirit, the conflict with the flesh, the fruit of the Spirit?

(C) Examine Colossians 3 — the putting off and putting on, the practical sanctification of every relationship?

(D) Move to the corporate dimension we previously identified — the Body of Christ, the Bride, the Temple, the Holy Nation?

(E) Another direction of your choosing?

A,B and C

We will examine all three together, in sequence — Romans 12, Galatians 5, and Colossians 3 — as they form the practical fabric of the indicative-imperative pattern Paul lays out in Romans 6-8.

Each passage carries the same DNA:

  • Indicative first — what God has done.
  • Imperative second — how we are to walk.
  • Practical application — to every sphere of life.

Let me unfold each in turn, drawing the threads together as we go.

PART 1 — ROMANS 12: THE LIVING SACRIFICE AND THE RENEWED MIND

The Transition

Paul has just concluded eleven chapters of doctrinal foundation — sin, justification, sanctification, life in the Spirit, the Father's sovereign plan in Israel and the nations. Then comes the great οὖν (therefore) at Romans 12:1 — the pivot from indicative to imperative on a grand scale.

Romans 12:1 — THE LIVING SACRIFICE

1599 Geneva:

"I beseech you therefore brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye give up your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable serving of God."

Observations of foundational importance

(1) Παρακαλῶ οὖν — "I therefore beseech you." The word οὖν (therefore) gathers up all eleven preceding chapters. The imperative is grounded in everything Paul has established. The believer is being asked to act on the basis of all that God has done.

(2) διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ — "by the mercies of God." The motivation for the imperative is the Father's mercies — the entire chain of mercy Paul has unfolded (chosen, called, justified, indwelt, sealed, secured). The believer is not motivated by fear or by the threat of loss, but by gratitude for mercy received.

(3) παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν — "present your bodies." This is the same verb παρίστημι Paul used in Romans 6:13 — "present yourselves to God." Now he specifies: present your bodies. Not your minds only, not your spirits only — your bodies. The physical, mortal, fleshly bodies in which we live our daily lives.

This is striking after Romans 7-8. Paul has just established that the body is mortal, weak, and the seat of competing desires. Yet this very body is to be presented as a sacrifice. The Father does not despise the body; He receives it as a holy offering.

(4) θυσίαν ζῶσαν — "a living sacrifice." A paradox. OT sacrifices were dead. The believer's sacrifice is alive — continually being offered, not slain once and consumed. The believer's life itself is the offering.

(5) ἁγίαν εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ — "holy, well-pleasing to God." The sacrifice is holy (set apart, dedicated) and well-pleasing to the Father. This is the believer's life when wholly given to the Father — a fragrant offering received with delight.

(6) τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ὑμῶν — "your reasonable service / spiritual worship."

λογικός can mean "rational, reasonable" (related to λόγος — reason, word) or "spiritual." The Geneva translates "reasonable serving." Either way, the meaning converges: in light of God's mercies, this whole-life presentation is the only reasonable response. It is not extreme; it is not optional; it is the proper, fitting, rational service of those who have received what the believer has received.

Practical Implications

(1) The believer's body is the place of worship. Not the church building. Not a sacred space. The body itself, presented to God, is the temple of acceptable worship. This dovetails with what we established in Part F — the believer's body is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 6:19).

(2) Worship is comprehensive, not compartmentalized. What we eat, what we wear, what we do with our hands, where we go with our feet, what we say with our tongues, what we think with our minds — all of this is the sphere of worship. There is no secular/sacred division in the believer's life. Every act of the body is potentially an act of worship.

(3) The presentation is to be definite. The aorist infinitive παραστῆσαι suggests a decisive act. The believer is to make a deliberate, conscious presentation of his body to God — not as a vague aspiration, but as a settled transaction. "Father, this body is Yours. Use it as You will."

Romans 12:2 — THE RENEWED MIND

1599 Geneva:

"And fashion not yourselves like unto this world, but be ye changed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what that good, that acceptable and perfect will of God is."

Observations of decisive practical importance

(1) μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ — "do not be conformed to this age."

The verb συσχηματίζεσθε is from σχῆμα — outward form, fashion, appearance. Present passive imperative — "stop being shaped to fit the pattern of this age."

The believer is shaped by something — the question is what. The world (this age) is constantly pressing its mold upon the believer through media, education, culture, fashion, expectation, ideology, advertising, conversation. To live without resistance is to be molded into the world's shape.

Paul commands: do not conform. Refuse the world's mold. Do not let this age dictate your outward form — your values, your priorities, your habits, your appearance, your patterns.

(2) ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε — "but be transformed."

μεταμορφοῦσθε is from μορφή — inward, essential form. This is the same root as the μεταμόρφωσις (metamorphosis) of the caterpillar to butterfly. A complete inward transformation of essential form. Present passive imperative — "keep being transformed."

The contrast is precise: do not let your outward σχῆμα be shaped by the world; let your inward μορφή be transformed by God. Outward form follows inward form. When the inner being is being transformed, the outer life is increasingly conformed not to this age but to Christ.

(3) τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός — "by the renewing of the mind."

The mechanism of transformation is the renewing of the mind (νοῦς).

The νοῦς is the believer's faculty of understanding, reasoning, perceiving, evaluating. It is the mind, but not in a narrow intellectual sense — it is the seat of one's whole orientation, values, and worldview.

The mind is renewed (ἀνακαίνωσις) — made new, fresh, reconstituted — by the Spirit working through the Word. As the believer feeds on Scripture, meditates on the Father's truth, beholds the Son's glory (2 Cor 3:18), and walks in the Spirit, his mind is progressively renewed.

The renewed mind is the inner mechanism of outer transformation. As the believer thinks differently — sees the world differently, evaluates differently, desires differently — his outward life is correspondingly transformed.

(4) εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ — "that you may prove / discern what the will of God is."

The result of the renewed mind: the ability to discern the Father's will. The unrenewed mind cannot discern God's will — it is set on the things of the flesh (Rom 8:5-7). The renewed mind, oriented by the Spirit, can recognize, evaluate, and confirm what is the Father's good, well-pleasing, and perfect will.

This is critically important for practical decision-making. The believer does not need a special revelation for every decision — though he must be open to such. The renewed mind, saturated with Scripture and yielded to the Spirit, can discern the Father's will in the ordinary course of life.

Practical Implications

(1) The believer must be actively engaged in mind-renewal. This requires:

  • Saturation in Scripture — reading, meditating, memorizing, studying the Word so that the renewed mind has the material from which to think God's thoughts after Him.
  • Resistance to worldly inputs — being discerning about what media, entertainment, conversation, and influences shape the mind.
  • Cultivation of holy thought patterns — "Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report... think on these things" (Phil 4:8 Geneva).
  • Walking in the Spirit — for it is the Spirit who applies the Word to renew the mind.
  • Fellowship with the saints — being shaped by godly community rather than by worldly community.

(2) The renewing of the mind is an ongoing process. The present tense μεταμορφοῦσθε suggests continuous action. The believer never reaches a point of completion in this life. He is always being transformed, always being renewed.

(3) Discernment grows. As the mind is renewed, the believer's ability to recognize the Father's will sharpens. What was once unclear becomes clearer. What was once a difficult judgment becomes an instinctive perception. The mature believer increasingly walks in the Father's will not by anguished deliberation but by Spirit-formed instinct.

Romans 12:3-21 — THE RENEWED MIND IN ACTION

The remainder of Romans 12 spells out what the renewed mind looks like in practice. We will not exposit every verse, but let us note the major themes.

Romans 12:3-8 — Sober Self-Assessment and Gifts

The renewed mind:

  • Does not think more highly of itself than it ought (v. 3) — humility before God and others.
  • Recognizes itself as a member of one body with diverse gifts (vv. 4-5).
  • Uses its gifts faithfully — prophecy, ministry, teaching, exhortation, giving, ruling, mercy (vv. 6-8).

This anticipates the corporate dimension we will examine later. But notice: the renewed mind has a sober estimation of self and a clear sense of place within the Body.

Romans 12:9-13 — Love in Practice

1599 Geneva:

"Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil, and cleave unto that which is good. Be affectioned to love one another with brotherly love: in giving honor, go one before another. ..."

The believer's love is to be unhypocritical — genuine, without pretense. The renewed mind hates evil and clings to good. It honors others. It is fervent in spirit, serving the Lord. It rejoices in hope, is patient in tribulation, continues steadfastly in prayer.

These are not isolated virtues; they are the natural fruit of a renewed mind living in the Spirit.

Romans 12:14-21 — Response to Enemies

1599 Geneva:

"Bless them which persecute you: bless, I say, and curse not. ... Recompense to no man evil for evil: procure things honest in the sight of all men. ... Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord. ... Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with goodness."

The most counter-cultural section of the chapter. The renewed mind:

  • Blesses persecutors rather than cursing them.
  • Does not repay evil for evil.
  • Does not avenge itself but leaves vengeance to the Father.
  • Overcomes evil with good.

This is impossible to the flesh. Only the renewed mind, empowered by the Spirit, can love enemies in this way. It is the very pattern of Christ on the cross.

PART 2 — GALATIANS 5: THE WALK BY THE SPIRIT AND THE WAR WITH THE FLESH

The Context

Paul has spent the first four chapters of Galatians defending the Gospel of grace against the Judaizers who insisted that Gentile believers must keep the Mosaic Law to be saved. Now, in chapters 5-6, he turns to the practical implications: how is the believer to live who is free from the law?

The answer is not antinomianism (lawlessness) but walking by the Spirit. The believer is free from the law as a system of justification, but he is by no means free to indulge the flesh. He is freed from law and sin into the Spirit's lordship.

Galatians 5:1 — STAND FAST IN FREEDOM

1599 Geneva:

"Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage."

Observation

Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν — "Christ has freed us." Aorist tense — the freedom is accomplished. The believer stands in this freedom. He does not negotiate it, does not earn it, does not re-create it. He stands in what Christ has won.

στήκετε οὖν — "stand therefore." The command is to stand firm. Not to revert to the yoke of bondage (the law as a system of justification or the flesh as a master).

Galatians 5:13-15 — FREEDOM, NOT LICENSE

1599 Geneva:

"For brethren, ye have been called unto liberty: only use not your liberty as an occasion unto the flesh: but by love serve one another. For all the Law is fulfilled in one word, which is this, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed least (lest) ye be consumed one of another."

Observation

The believer is called to freedom — but freedom is not license. The believer is freed from the flesh's tyranny, not freed for the flesh's gratification. The believer's freedom is fulfilled in loving service to one another.

The whole law is fulfilled in love (citing Lev 19:18) — not because the believer is under the law for justification, but because the believer, walking by the Spirit, produces what the law required.

Galatians 5:16-17 — THE FOUNDATIONAL COMMAND

1599 Geneva:

"Then I say, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary one to another, so that ye cannot do the same things that ye would."

Observations of decisive importance

(1) Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε — "walk by the Spirit." Present imperative — continuous walking. The Christian life is not a one-time decision; it is a continuous walk.

The dative Πνεύματι is instrumental — "by means of the Spirit." The Spirit is both the path and the power of the walk. The believer walks by the Spirit's leading and in the Spirit's empowering.

(2) The promise: ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε — "you shall by no means fulfill the lust of the flesh."

οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive is the strongest possible negation in Greek — "absolutely not, by no means, in no way." The promise is absolute: the believer who walks by the Spirit will not fulfill the flesh's lust.

This is the practical answer to every besetting sin. The believer does not defeat the flesh by attacking it directly; he defeats it by walking in the Spirit — at which point the flesh's lust is bypassed.

(3) ἡ γὰρ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος, τὸ δὲ Πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός — "the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh."

Two opposing principles within the believer. This is honest. The flesh (the remaining principle of sin in our mortal members) does not disappear at conversion. It lusts (ἐπιθυμεῖ — desires, craves) against the Spirit. And the Spirit lusts against the flesh — opposes it, contradicts it, fights it.

These are contrary (ἀλλήλοις ἀντίκειται). The believer cannot serve both. The believer's life is a constant choice — who will I walk with today, this hour, this moment? The Spirit or the flesh?

Galatians 5:19-21 — THE WORKS OF THE FLESH

1599 Geneva:

"Moreover the works of the flesh are manifest, which are adultery, fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, debate, emulations, wrath, contentions, seditions, heresies, Envy, murthers (murders), drunkenness, gluttony, and such like, whereof I tell you before, as I also have told you before, that they which do such things, shall not inherit the kingdom of God."

Observations

(1) φανερά — "manifest, plain to see." The works of the flesh are obvious. They are not hidden mysteries; they are visible in the lives of those who walk by the flesh.

(2) The list is comprehensive — covering:

  • Sexual immorality (πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία, ἀσέλγεια).
  • False religion (εἰδωλολατρία, φαρμακεία — idolatry, sorcery).
  • Relational disorder (ἔχθραι, ἔρις, ζῆλος, θυμοί, ἐριθεῖαι, διχοστασίαι, αἱρέσεις, φθόνοι — hatred, strife, jealousy, outbursts of wrath, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions, envy).
  • Lifestyle excess (μέθαι, κῶμοι — drunkenness, revelries).

The list is not exhaustive — "and such like" (καὶ τὰ ὅμοια τούτοις) — but illustrative. The flesh produces these kinds of things wherever it reigns.

(3) The warning: "They which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God."

This is sobering. A pattern of life characterized by the works of the flesh is incompatible with citizenship in the kingdom. Paul is not saying a believer who falls into one of these sins is lost; he is saying that those whose lives are characterized by these patterns demonstrate they are not in the Spirit's possession.

The mark of a true believer is not the absence of all sin (we still battle the flesh), but the direction of life — being increasingly turned away from these patterns by the Spirit's work.

Galatians 5:22-23 — THE FRUIT OF THE SPIRIT

1599 Geneva:

"But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long suffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no Law."

Observations of supreme importance

(1) Note: ὁ καρπός — singular, not "the fruits." It is one fruit with nine facets. The Spirit's fruit is a single integrated character — not a buffet from which we can select preferences.

(2) Compare with the works of the flesh. The flesh produces "works" (ἔργα — plural, fragmented, disordered acts). The Spirit produces "fruit" (καρπός — singular, organic, integrated growth).

This contrast is profound: the flesh manufactures (works); the Spirit grows (fruit). The flesh produces by effort; the Spirit produces by organic life within. The fruit cannot be forced; it grows naturally from a healthy union with the Spirit.

(3) The nine facets:

  • ἀγάπη — love (sacrificial, willed love)
  • χαρά — joy (the deep joy of the Lord)
  • εἰρήνη — peace (the peace of God that surpasses understanding)
  • μακροθυμία — long-suffering / patience with people
  • χρηστότης — kindness, useful service
  • ἀγαθωσύνη — goodness, moral excellence
  • πίστις — faith / faithfulness
  • πραΰτης — meekness, gentle strength
  • ἐγκράτεια — self-control

These are the character of Christ. Each one was perfectly displayed in Him. As the Spirit conforms the believer to the Son's image (Rom 8:29), these qualities increasingly appear in the believer's life — not by his manufacturing them, but by the Spirit's growing them.

(4) κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἔστιν νόμος — "against such things there is no law."

A wonderful note. No law condemns these qualities. The believer who walks in the Spirit and produces this fruit is automatically in fulfillment of every law's righteous demand — without being under the law.

Galatians 5:24-25 — THE CRUCIFICATION OF THE FLESH AND THE WALK BY THE SPIRIT

1599 Geneva:

"For they that are Christ's, have crucified the flesh, with the affections and the lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit."

Observations

(1) οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὴν σάρκα ἐσταύρωσαν — "those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh." Aorist tense — a completed past act.

This recapitulates Romans 6 in compressed form. The flesh has been crucified with its passions and lusts. The believer's identification with Christ's cross includes the crucifixion of the flesh.

(2) εἰ ζῶμεν Πνεύματι, Πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν — "if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit."

The indicative-imperative pattern again, in compressed form:

  • Indicative: "We live by the Spirit" (an established reality).
  • Imperative: "Let us walk by the Spirit" (the corresponding action).

The verb στοιχῶμεν is military — "march in step, walk in line, keep in formation." The believer who lives by the Spirit is to march in step with the Spirit — keeping in line with His leading, His pace, His direction.

PART 3 — COLOSSIANS 3: THE PUTTING OFF AND PUTTING ON

The Context

Paul has just spent Colossians 1-2 establishing the supremacy and fullness of Christ — Creator, Sustainer, Head of the Body, the Image of the invisible God, in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. He has warned against false philosophies that would diminish Christ. Now in chapter 3, he turns to the practical implications: since you are united with this Christ, here is how you walk.

Colossians 3:1-4 — THE INDICATIVE FOUNDATION

1599 Geneva:

"If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth at the right hand of God. Set your affections on things which are above, and not on things which are on the earth. For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. When Christ which is our life shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory."

Observations

We touched on these verses earlier in our examination of identification. Now we see them in their practical-imperative context.

(1) The indicative reality (vv. 1, 3-4):

  • You have been raised with Christ.
  • You died.
  • Your life is hidden with Christ in God.
  • You will appear with Him in glory.

These are the established facts of identification.

(2) The imperatives flow from the indicative:

  • τὰ ἄνω ζητεῖτε — "seek the things above." Present imperative — keep seeking.
  • τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε — "set your mind on the things above." Present imperative — keep your mind oriented upward.

The believer's orientation is to be upward — toward where Christ is. This is not other-worldly escapism; it is eternal perspective in the midst of earthly life.

(3) The Connecting Word: Notice the οὖν (therefore) in v. 1. Because you have been raised (indicative), therefore seek the things above (imperative). The pattern is exactly the same as Romans 6, 8, 12.

Colossians 3:5-9 — PUTTING OFF

1599 Geneva:

"Mortify therefore your members which are on the earth, fornication, uncleanness, the inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness which is idolatry. For the which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience. Wherein ye also walked once, when ye lived in them. But now put ye away even all these things, wrath, anger, maliciousness, cursed speaking, filthy speaking, out of your mouth. Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his works,"

Observations

(1) Νεκρώσατε — "put to death." Aorist imperative — a definitive action. The believer is to put to death the earthly members.

This is parallel to Romans 8:13 — "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body." The believer's responsibility is active — to put to death — but the empowering is the Spirit's.

(2) First list — sins of corrupt desire:

  • πορνεία — sexual immorality
  • ἀκαθαρσία — uncleanness
  • πάθος — passion (especially shameful)
  • ἐπιθυμίαν κακήν — evil desire
  • πλεονεξίαν — covetousness, which is idolatry

These are the sins of disordered desire — wanting what is not ours to have.

(3) Second list — sins of corrupt relationship:

  • ὀργήν — wrath
  • θυμόν — anger (sudden outbursts)
  • κακίαν — malice
  • βλασφημίαν — slander
  • αἰσχρολογίαν — filthy/abusive speech

These are the sins that destroy relationships within the Body.

(4) μὴ ψεύδεσθε εἰς ἀλλήλους — "do not lie to one another." A specific application of the relational sins. Lying is incompatible with the new identity in Christ.

(5) ἀπεκδυσάμενοι τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον — "having put off the old man."

The verb ἀπεκδυσάμενοι is aorist middle — a completed action. The old man has been put off. The believer is not striving to put off what is still part of his identity; he is walking in the reality that the old man has already been put off in Christ.

This is the indicative undergirding the imperative. Because the old man has been put off (positionally), therefore put off these practices that belonged to him (practically).

Colossians 3:10-11 — PUTTING ON THE NEW MAN

1599 Geneva:

"And have put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him. Where is neither Grecian nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond, free: But Christ is all, and in all things."

Observations

(1) ἐνδυσάμενοι τὸν νέον — "having put on the new [man]." Again aorist middle — a completed action. The new man has been put on.

(2) τὸν ἀνακαινούμενον εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν κατ᾽ εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος αὐτόν — "being renewed unto knowledge according to the image of Him who created him."

The new man is being continually renewed (present participle) unto full knowledge of the One in whose image he was created.

The image is Christ Himself — the perfect Image of the invisible God (Col 1:15). The new man is being progressively renewed to fully bear that image.

(3) ὅπου οὐκ ἔνι... — "where there is not..." — in the new man, the old divisions are abolished:

  • Greek and Jew
  • Circumcised and uncircumcised
  • Barbarian, Scythian
  • Slave, free

ἀλλὰ τὰ πάντα καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν Χριστός — "but Christ is all and in all."

In the new humanity that is the Body of Christ, Christ is all — the unifying reality that transcends every former division. This anticipates the corporate dimension we will examine later.

Colossians 3:12-17 — THE NEW MAN IN PRACTICE

1599 Geneva:

"Now therefore as the elect of God holy and beloved, put on the bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, long suffering, Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel to another: even as Christ forgave, even so do ye. And above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness. And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which ye are called in one body, and be ye thankful."

Observations

(1) Ἐνδύσασθε οὖν — "therefore put on." The imperative flows from the identity: as elect, holy, and beloved of God, you are to put on these characteristics.

(2) The garments of the new man:

  • σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ — "bowels of mercies" (deep, visceral compassion)
  • χρηστότητα — kindness
  • ταπεινοφροσύνην — humility
  • πραΰτητα — meekness
  • μακροθυμίαν — long-suffering
  • ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων — bearing with one another
  • χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς — forgiving one another (literally, "granting grace")

(3) The pattern: καθὼς καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς — "as the Lord forgave you, so also you."

The believer forgives because and as he has been forgiven. The Father's gracious treatment in Christ becomes the pattern of our treatment of others.

(4) ἐπὶ πᾶσιν δὲ τούτοις τὴν ἀγάπην, ὅ ἐστιν σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος — "and above all these things, love, which is the bond of perfectness."

Love is the binding garment that holds all the others together. Without love, kindness becomes flattery, humility becomes self-loathing, patience becomes mere endurance. Love is the unifying principle.

(5) ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Χριστοῦ βραβευέτω ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν — "let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts."

The verb βραβευέτω is from βραβεύς — an umpire, an arbiter. Christ's peace is to be the umpire in the believer's heart — settling disputes, making decisions, ruling over conflicts. When peace departs from the heart, it is often the signal that something is wrong in our direction.

Colossians 3:18-4:1 — PRACTICAL SANCTIFICATION IN RELATIONSHIPS

1599 Geneva (summary):

"Wives, submit yourselves unto your husbands, as it is comely in the Lord. ... Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter unto them. ... Children, obey your parents in all thing (things) for that is well pleasing unto the Lord. ... Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, least (lest) they be discouraged. ... Servants, be obedient unto them that are your masters according to the flesh, in all things, not with eye service as men pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God. ... Ye masters, do unto your servants, that which is just, and equal, knowing that ye also have a master in heaven."

Observation

The practical sanctification reaches into every sphere of relationship:

  • Marriage: wives submit, husbands love.
  • Family: children obey, fathers do not provoke.
  • Work/economic relationships: servants serve as unto the Lord, masters treat servants justly.

The renewed mind transforms every relationship. The Father's purposes for family, work, and social relations are honored not because of law but because the new man, indwelt by the Spirit, walks in love.

Colossians 3:17 — THE GOVERNING PRINCIPLE

1599 Geneva:

"And whatsoever ye shall do, in word or deed, do all in the Name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God even the Father by him."

Observation

The single, governing principle of all practical Christian living:

  • Whatever you do — in word or deed — do all in the Name of the Lord Jesus.
  • Give thanks to God the Father through Him.

Every action of the believer's life is to be done in the Name of the Lord Jesus — that is, as one belonging to Him, representing Him, acting in His authority, for His glory. And every action is to be accompanied by thanksgiving to the Father through Him.

This single verse captures the comprehensive nature of Christian practice. No part of life is excluded. No moment is secular. Every word and deed is to be in His Name and to the Father's glory.

GRAND SYNTHESIS — THE THREE PASSAGES TOGETHER

Romans 12, Galatians 5, and Colossians 3 are not three different teachings — they are three angles on the same reality: how the indicative of who we are in Christ produces the imperative of how we walk.

The Common Pattern

ElementRomans 12Galatians 5Colossians 3
Indicative foundationGod's mercies (11 chapters of doctrine)Christ has freed us (1:1-4:31)Raised with Christ; died; life hidden with Him
Pivot wordοὖν (12:1)οὖν (5:1, implied throughout)οὖν (3:1, 5, 12)
Body presentationPresent your bodies (12:1)Walk by the Spirit (5:16)Mortify your members (3:5)
Mind renewalRenewing of the mind (12:2)Mind set on Spirit (implied)Set affection on things above (3:1-2)
Discernment of willProve what is good will of God (12:2)Led by the Spirit (5:18)Walk in wisdom (3:16)
Putting offCast off works of darknessCrucified the flesh (5:24)Put off the old man (3:9)
Putting onChrist's characterFruit of the Spirit (5:22-23)Put on the new man (3:10-14)
Love as governingLove without dissimulation (12:9)Through love serve one another (5:13)Love is the bond of perfectness (3:14)
Comprehensive scopeAll relationships, including enemiesEvery part of lifeEvery sphere — marriage, family, work

The Single Practical Theology

What emerges from all three passages is one coherent doctrine of practical sanctification:

The believer who has died with Christ, been raised with Him, is seated with Him at the Father's right hand, and is indwelt by the Spirit — this believer is to walk in newness of life by:

  1. Presenting his body as a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1) / mortifying his earthly members (Col 3:5) — the comprehensive yielding of the physical body to God.
  1. Being renewed in the mind (Rom 12:2; Col 3:10) — the ongoing transformation of the inner orientation by the Word and the Spirit.
  1. Walking by the Spirit (Gal 5:16) — depending moment by moment on the Spirit's leading and empowering.
  1. Putting off the works of the old man (Col 3:5-9; Gal 5:19-21) — actively refusing the patterns of the flesh.
  1. Putting on the new man (Col 3:10-14) — actively cultivating the patterns of Christ's character.
  1. Walking in love (Rom 12:9-21; Gal 5:13-14; Col 3:14) — the unifying principle of all Christian practice.
  1. Doing all in the Name of the Lord Jesus, with thanksgiving to the Father (Col 3:17) — the comprehensive governing principle.

The Practical Modern Application

For the modern believer, this means:

In the morning: Reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God. Present your body to the Father as a living sacrifice. Set your mind on things above. Open the Word and feed the renewing process.

Throughout the day: Walk by the Spirit. Yield to His leading. Put off the works of the flesh as they arise. Put on the characteristics of Christ. Do every word and deed in the Name of the Lord Jesus, with thanksgiving.

In relationships: Love without dissimulation. Bless those who persecute. Forgive as Christ has forgiven. Honor your spouse, parents, children, employer, employees, brethren. Be at peace with all men so far as it depends on you. Overcome evil with good.

In the mind: Resist the world's mold. Embrace the Spirit's transformation. Think on what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report. Take every thought captive to obey Christ. Renew the mind through Scripture, prayer, and fellowship.

In moments of failure: Return immediately to the reckoning. Confess. Trust the cleansing blood. Receive forgiveness. Get up and walk again. Do not despair; do not abandon the walk; do not let one failure define the day.

In suffering: Recognize the Father's purpose — conformity to the Son. Trust that all things work together for good. Hold fast the unshakable hope. Look beyond present sufferings to the coming glory.

In all things: Live as one who belongs to the Father, walks in the Son, is indwelt by the Spirit, and is destined for glory. You are not who you were. You are in Christ. Walk worthy.

A CLOSING OBSERVATION

Brother, what we have surveyed in these three passages is the genius of the New Testament's ethic. It is not a system of rules to be followed; it is a life to be lived out of who we already are. It is not the achievement of an unreal status; it is the working out of what is positionally true.

The modern believer who walks in this reality is:

  • Free — from law as a means of justification, from the flesh as a master, from the world as a mold.
  • Empowered — by the indwelling Spirit who produces what the believer cannot manufacture.
  • Oriented — toward the things above, where Christ is seated.
  • Renewed — in the mind, progressively conformed to the Son's image.
  • Engaged — in active putting off and putting on, by the Spirit's power.
  • In love — the unifying principle of all Christian practice.
  • In community — for the new humanity transcends every former division.
  • In every sphere — for nothing in the believer's life is exempt from the Lordship of Christ.

This is what the Father's eternal purpose looks like in daily practice. This is what it means to be a child of the Father, in the Beloved Son, by the indwelling Spirit, walking by faith until He appears.

A QUESTION FOR YOU

Where would you have us go next?

(A) Move now to the corporate dimension — the Body of Christ, the Bride of Christ, the Temple of God, the Holy Nation, the Royal Priesthood?

(B) Examine the eschatological consummation — the resurrection of the body, the marriage of the Lamb, the new heavens and new earth, the inheritance of the kingdom?

(C) A specific aspect of the practical walk you wish to examine more carefully — perhaps prayer, the use of Scripture, the believer's response to specific kinds of trials, or the spiritual disciplines?

(D) Another direction of your choosing?

Yes, let’s do a thorough (exhaustive) examination of all relevant aspects of C above

I will pick up from where we left off and continue through the remaining sections of the spiritual disciplines and responses by which the believer cooperates with the Spirit's work.

Completing the Lord's Prayer Pattern

The pattern Jesus gave provides the believer with six categories of prayer:

CategoryPetitionMeaning
Adoration"Our Father... hallowed be Thy Name"Worshipping the Father and reverencing His Name
Kingdom"Thy kingdom come"Submitting to and praying for His reign
Surrender"Thy will be done"Yielding our will to His
Provision"Give us this day our daily bread"Asking for daily needs
Confession/Forgiveness"Forgive us our debts... as we also forgive"Maintenance of fellowship through confession
Deliverance"Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil"Asking for protection from sin and the evil one

This is the architecture of healthy prayer. Notice the priority: God's glory and kingdom first (three petitions), our needs second (three petitions). The believer is taught to think God-first, kingdom-first, and only then bring his own needs.

Praying in the Spirit

We examined under Romans 8 that the Spirit intercedes for us in our weakness. But the believer is also commanded to pray in the Spirit:

Ephesians 6:18 — Geneva 1599:

"And pray always with all manner prayer and supplication in the Spirit: and watch thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all Saints,"

Jude 20-21 — Geneva 1599:

"But, ye beloved, edify yourselves in your most holy faith, praying in the holy Ghost, And keep yourselves in the love of God..."

Observations

To pray in the Spirit means:

  • Praying in the Spirit's empowerment rather than in the flesh's eloquence.
  • Praying in alignment with the Spirit's leading rather than according to our own desires alone.
  • Praying with the Spirit interceding through us — sometimes with words, sometimes with groanings beyond words (Rom 8:26).
  • Praying with the Spirit's witness that we are children, freely calling on the Father (Rom 8:15-16).

This is not a special technique; it is the normal mode of Christian prayer. The believer prays in the Spirit because the Spirit indwells him and prays through him.

The Modes of Prayer

The NT presents several distinct modes of prayer the believer is to practice:

1. Petition (αἴτησις) — Asking for Specific Needs

Matthew 7:7-11 — Geneva 1599:

"Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and ye shall find: knock, and it shall be opened unto you..."

The Father invites our requests. Three present imperatives — ask, seek, knock — all in continuous tense. We are to keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. The Father delights to give good gifts to His children.

2. Thanksgiving (εὐχαριστία)

1 Thessalonians 5:18 — Geneva 1599:

"In all things give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you."

In all things — not for all things in the sense of celebrating evil, but in the midst of all things — give thanks. Thanksgiving is the will of God for the believer.

3. Intercession (ἔντευξις) — Praying for Others

1 Timothy 2:1-2 — Geneva 1599:

"I exhort therefore, that first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made for all men: For Kings, and for all that are in authority..."

The believer is to intercede for all men — for the lost, for fellow believers, for rulers and authorities, for enemies, for the suffering. Intercession is one of the highest privileges of the Christian life.

4. Confession (ὁμολογία)

We will examine this fully in its own section, but it is a major mode of prayer — agreeing with God about our sin.

5. Adoration / Worship

The lifting up of the heart in praise to the Father — which we will examine more fully in the worship section.

6. Lament

The honest expression to the Father of grief, distress, perplexity, even questioning — modeled in the Psalms and by the Son in Gethsemane and on the cross. The believer is not required to pretend to feelings he does not have; he is invited to bring his real state before the Father.

The Posture of Prayer

Persistence

Luke 18:1 — Geneva 1599:

"And he spake also a parable unto them, to this end, that they ought always to pray, and not to wax faint,"

The parable of the persistent widow teaches that the believer is to pray always and not faint. Some answers require persistent asking over time. The Father is not slow; He is wise — and He uses delayed answers to deepen our dependence.

Faith

Mark 11:24 — Geneva 1599:

"...Whatsoever ye desire when ye pray, believe that ye shall have it, and it shall be done unto you."

Prayer is to be offered in faith — trusting the Father's character and promises. Not faith in our prayers, but faith in the One to whom we pray.

According to His Will

1 John 5:14-15 — Geneva 1599:

"And this is that assurance, that we have in him, that if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us..."

Prayer is to be according to His will. Not every request is granted — but every request offered in submission to His will is heard. The believer prays "Thy will be done" — confident that the Father's will is best, even when His will differs from our preferences.

In Jesus' Name

John 14:13-14 — Geneva 1599:

"And whatsoever ye ask in my Name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If ye shall ask any thing in my Name, I will do it."

Prayer is offered in Jesus' Name — that is, on the basis of His person, His mediation, and His authority. Not as a magical formula appended to prayers, but as the recognition that all access to the Father is through the Son.

With Thanksgiving

Philippians 4:6-7 — Geneva 1599:

"Be nothing careful, but in all things let your requests be showed unto God in prayer, and supplication with giving of thanks. And the peace of God which passeth all understanding, shall preserve your hearts..."

Prayer with thanksgiving is the antidote to anxiety. The promise: peace that surpasses understanding will guard the heart.

Practical Implications for the Modern Believer

1. Establish a regular time of prayer — daily, ideally in the morning. Not as legalistic duty, but as joyful communion. The believer who waits to "feel like" praying will rarely pray.

2. Use the Lord's Prayer pattern — let Jesus' template shape the architecture of your daily prayer. Adoration → Kingdom → Surrender → Provision → Confession → Deliverance.

3. Pray Scripture back to the Father — pray through the Psalms, pray through Paul's prayers (Eph 1:15-23; 3:14-21; Phil 1:9-11; Col 1:9-12). Let the Word shape your prayers.

4. Pray with persistence — do not abandon prayer when answers delay. The Father uses delay to deepen us.

5. Pray for others — keep a list of those for whom you intercede: family, brethren, enemies, rulers, missionaries, the lost.

6. Pray throughout the day — "pray without ceasing" (1 Thess 5:17) means maintaining a continuous attitude of God-consciousness, with frequent brief turning of the heart to Him.

7. Pray with thanksgiving — even in trial, give thanks for what you have received, for who He is, for the hope set before you.

8. Pray honestly — bring your real state. The Father does not need pious phrases; He desires the honest heart.

PART 2 — THE WORD OF GOD: THE RENEWING OF THE MIND

We established under Romans 12:2 that the believer is transformed by the renewing of the mind. The primary instrument of this renewal is the Word of God applied by the Spirit.

The Nature of Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16-17:

"For the whole Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable to teach, to convince (convict), to correct, and to instruct in righteousness, That the man of God may be absolute (complete, perfect), being made perfect unto all good works."

Observations of foundational importance

(1) θεόπνευστος — "God-breathed." Scripture is the very breath of God — proceeding from Him as our own breath proceeds from us. This single word establishes the divine origin and authority of the Word.

(2) Four practical uses:

  • διδασκαλίαν — teaching (showing what is true).
  • ἐλεγμόν — convicting / reproof (showing what is wrong).
  • ἐπανόρθωσιν — correction / setting straight (showing how to get right).
  • παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ — training in righteousness (showing how to stay right).

The Word makes the believer complete — ἄρτιος (fit, complete, fitted) — equipped for every good work.

The Word's Active Power

Hebrews 4:12:

"For the word of God is lively (alive), and mighty in operation, and sharper than any two edged sword, and entereth through, even unto the dividing asunder of the soul and the spirit, and of the joints, and the marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts, and the intents of the heart."

Observation

The Word of God is ζῶν (living) — alive, active, not merely a printed text. It is ἐνεργής (energetically working) — accomplishing what God sends it to do. It penetrates beyond the surface to discern thoughts and intents of the heart.

This is why the Word renews the mind. The Spirit uses the living Word to penetrate, expose, instruct, and transform.

The Modes of Engaging the Word

1. Reading

The believer should read the Word regularly — substantial portions, not merely scattered verses. The whole counsel of God comes through engagement with the whole text.

2. Hearing

Romans 10:17:

"Then faith is by hearing, and hearing by the word of God."

Faith comes by hearing the Word. The believer benefits from preaching, teaching, and the audible reading of Scripture — both privately (reading aloud) and corporately (in the assembly).

3. Meditating

Psalm 1:1-2 LXX (Ps 1:1-2 MT):

Happy the man … Rather, his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night. — Psalm 1:1-2, NETS

μελετάω — to meditate, ponder, chew over, mutter to oneself. The blessed man meditates on the Law day and night. Meditation is the slow, deliberate pondering of a text — turning it over, asking what it means, applying it to one's life, allowing it to penetrate.

4. Memorizing

Psalm 118:11 LXX (Ps 119:11 MT):

In my heart I hid your sayings so that I may not sin against you. — Psalm 118:11 LXX (= MT 119:11), NETS

The Word hidden in the heart guards against sin. Memorized Scripture becomes available to the Spirit's recall in moments of temptation, trial, and decision.

5. Studying

The serious examination of Scripture — comparing passage with passage, examining the Greek and Hebrew where helpful, considering context. Per our maxims, this is the discipline of letting Scripture interpret itself by two or more witnesses.

6. Applying / Obeying

James 1:22-25:

"And be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves..."

The Word is given to be done, not merely heard. The believer who hears but does not do deceives himself. The renewing of the mind issues in renewed living.

Practical Implications

1. Establish a regular reading plan — daily, substantial portions. Many find systematic reading through the entire Bible over a year or two beneficial.

2. Meditate on key passages — slow down. Read less, think more. Let the Spirit illuminate.

3. Memorize strategic passages — psalms, key NT verses on identification with Christ, promises, exhortations.

4. Study with the LXX where you are able — per our maxims, this is the text Jesus and the Apostles used.

5. Apply what you read — ask: what does this mean? what does it require? how does it call me to walk?

6. Read in community — the Word is read in the assembly, and small-group study deepens understanding.

7. Pray Scripture — let the Word shape your prayers. The Psalms are especially helpful.

8. Beware of substituting commentary for text — read the Bible itself first. Commentaries can help, but they are servants of the text, not replacements for it.

PART 3 — WORSHIP AND PRAISE

Worship is the believer's response of adoration to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. It is both an inward attitude and outward expression.

The Foundation: Worship in Spirit and Truth

John 4:23-24 — Geneva 1599:

"But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit, and truth: for the Father requireth even such to worship him. God is a Spirit, and they that worship him, must worship him in spirit and truth."

Observations

We already examined this passage extensively under Part E (the Father as Eternal Spirit). Let us now note its implications for worship:

(1) Worship is to the Father. Jesus identifies the Father as the recipient of true worship. This honors our foundation.

(2) Worship is in Spirit and truth.

  • In Spirit — in the believer's regenerated spirit, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, not merely outward observance.
  • In truth — in conformity with the truth God has revealed, not in falsehood or self-invented worship.

(3) The Father seeks such worshippers. The Father is not indifferent. He seeks those who worship Him truly.

The Sacrifice of Praise

Hebrews 13:15 — Geneva 1599:

Let us therefore by him offer the sacrifice of praise always to God, that is, the fruit of the lips, which confess his Name.

Observation

Praise is a sacrifice — offered through Him (the Son) to God (the Father). The "fruit of the lips" confessing His Name is acceptable to the Father through the Son.

This is the new covenant fulfillment of the OT sacrificial system: not animals on an altar, but praise from the heart of the redeemed, offered through the Mediator.

The Modes of Worship

Ephesians 5:18-20 — Geneva 1599:

...but be fulfilled (filled) with the Spirit, Speaking unto yourselves in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual songs, singing, and making melody to the Lord in your hearts, Giving thanks always for all things unto God even the Father, in the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

Observations

(1) Worship is a fruit of being filled with the Spirit. The Spirit-filled believer naturally speaks in spiritual songs, sings, gives thanks.

(2) Three categories of song:

  • ψαλμοί — psalms (the OT Psalter).
  • ὕμνοι — hymns (compositions of praise).
  • ᾠδαὶ πνευματικαί — spiritual songs (Spirit-prompted songs).

(3) Singing is to the Lord — in the heart. External singing is the overflow of internal melody. The heart sings first; the lips follow.

(4) Thanksgiving in all things, in His Name, to the Father. The pattern again: through the Son, to the Father.

Worship in Daily Life

Worship is not confined to formal services. The whole of life is worship, as Romans 12:1 established. But there are particular acts of worship:

  • Daily morning thanksgiving — beginning the day with adoration.
  • Singing throughout the day — psalms, hymns, spiritual songs as the Spirit prompts.
  • Acknowledging God in all decisions — "In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths" (Prov 3:6 Geneva).
  • Gathering with the saints — corporate worship in the assembly.
  • The Lord's Supper — the great act of remembering and communing.
  • Acts of service — service rendered to others as worship to the Father.

PART 4 — FELLOWSHIP WITH THE SAINTS

The believer is not designed for isolation. The Father has placed him in the Body of Christ, where he both ministers to others and is ministered to.

The Foundation: We Belong to One Another

Romans 12:5 — Geneva 1599:

"So we being many are one body in Christ, and every one, one anothers members."

The believer is a member of the Body — and members of one another. The body image insists on mutual interdependence.

The Necessity of Assembling

Hebrews 10:24-25 — Geneva 1599:

"And let us consider one another, to provoke unto love, and to good works, Not forsaking the fellowship that we have among ourselves, as the manner of some is: but let us exhort one another, and that so much the more, because ye see that the day draweth near."

Observations

(1) The believers are to consider one another — paying attention to one another's needs.

(2) The purpose is to stir up love and good works — to provoke one another (παροξυσμός — a sharp stirring up) toward what is good.

(3) Negative command: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together." Some were already abandoning the gathering. The author warns against this.

(4) Positive command: "Exhorting one another." The believers are to encourage and admonish one another.

(5) Urgency: "As ye see the day approaching." The Lord's return makes faithful gathering more urgent, not less.

The "One Another" Commands

The NT contains over fifty "one another" commands — instructions for how believers are to relate to one another in the Body. Major examples:

  • Love one another (John 13:34; Rom 12:10; 13:8; 1 Thess 4:9; 1 Pet 1:22; 1 John 3:11, 23; 4:7, 11-12).
  • Forgive one another (Eph 4:32; Col 3:13).
  • Bear with one another (Eph 4:2; Col 3:13).
  • Bear one another's burdens (Gal 6:2).
  • Comfort one another (1 Thess 4:18; 5:11).
  • Encourage / exhort one another (1 Thess 5:11; Heb 3:13; 10:25).
  • Build up one another (Rom 14:19; 1 Thess 5:11).
  • Serve one another (Gal 5:13; 1 Pet 4:10).
  • Submit to one another (Eph 5:21; 1 Pet 5:5).
  • Honor one another (Rom 12:10).
  • Be hospitable to one another (1 Pet 4:9).
  • Pray for one another (James 5:16).
  • Confess sins to one another (James 5:16).
  • Teach and admonish one another (Col 3:16).
  • Greet one another (Rom 16:16; 1 Cor 16:20; 2 Cor 13:12; 1 Pet 5:14).
  • Do not bite and devour one another (Gal 5:15).
  • Do not lie to one another (Col 3:9).
  • Do not speak evil of one another (James 4:11).

This is the texture of biblical fellowship. Christianity is not a solitary pursuit; it is a body life.

Practical Implications

1. Be committed to a local assembly. The believer needs the regular gathering of the saints — for teaching, worship, fellowship, the Lord's Supper, prayer, and mutual encouragement.

2. Develop deep relationships with a few fellow believers — those with whom you can pray, confess sin, bear burdens, exhort.

3. Use your gifts to serve the Body — every believer has gifts (Rom 12; 1 Cor 12; Eph 4; 1 Pet 4:10-11). Discover yours and use them.

4. Be a source of encouragement. In a world of discouragement, the believer who consistently encourages is a deep gift to the Body.

5. Bear with weaknesses. Every believer has weaknesses, immaturities, and failures. Bear with one another in patience.

6. Resist factionalism, gossip, and divisive speech. These are the work of the flesh and destroy the Body's unity.

7. Submit to godly leaders (Heb 13:17). The Father has appointed shepherds for the flock; submit to their oversight as those who watch for your souls.

PART 5 — THE LORD'S SUPPER

The Lord's Supper is the appointed act of remembrance and communion that the Lord Himself instituted on the night of His betrayal.

The Institution

1 Corinthians 11:23-26 — Geneva 1599:

"...That the Lord Jesus in the night when he was betrayed, took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do ye in remembrance of me. After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the New Testament in my blood: this do as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as ye shall eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye show the Lord's death till he come."

Observations

(1) Three elements:

  • The Bread — representing His body broken for us.
  • The Cup — representing the New Covenant in His blood.
  • The Remembrance — "in remembrance of Me" (εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν).

(2) The proclamation — "you show the Lord's death till He come." The Supper is both a remembrance of the past (His death) and a proclamation toward the future (until He comes).

(3) The frequency — "as often as you drink it." The NT does not prescribe a specific frequency. The early church appears to have observed it frequently — perhaps weekly (Acts 20:7).

The Self-Examination

1 Corinthians 11:27-29 — Geneva 1599:

"Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink the cup of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Let every man therefore examine himself, and so let him eat of this bread, and drink of this cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh his own damnation, because he discerneth not the Lord's body."

Observations

(1) Self-examination is commanded — δοκιμαζέτω ἑαυτόν — "let a man examine himself" (the 1599 print reads, "Let every man therefore examine himself"). Before partaking, the believer is to examine his own heart.

(2) Eating unworthily is the danger — not because the believer is worthy in himself (none are), but because the manner of partaking can be unworthy — without faith, without discernment, in unconfessed sin, in division from the brethren.

(3) Discerning the body — recognizing the significance of the broken body of the Lord, and (in context of 1 Cor 11) recognizing the Body of Christ which is the Church (the Corinthians were divided and treating one another shamefully at the Supper).

Practical Implications

1. Approach the Supper with reverence. It is not a casual meal but a sacred remembrance.

2. Examine yourself before partaking. Confess known sin. Reconcile with brethren. Come with faith.

3. Use the Supper as an occasion of fresh consecration. Each remembrance is an opportunity to renew your dedication to the One who died for you.

4. Look both backward and forward. Backward to His death; forward to His return.

5. Recognize the Body. The Supper is a corporate act — celebrated with the Body of Christ.

PART 6 — WATCHFULNESS AND RESISTANCE OF TEMPTATION

The believer is in spiritual conflict. The Christian life requires vigilance.

The Reality of the Conflict

1 Peter 5:8-9 — Geneva 1599:

"Be sober, and watch: for your adversary the devil as a roaring lion walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: Whom resist steadfast in the faith..."

Observations

(1) Two commands: be sober (νήψατε — clear-minded, self-controlled) and watch (γρηγορήσατε — alert, vigilant).

(2) The adversary is real — the devil prowls like a roaring lion seeking prey.

(3) The response: resist him steadfast in the faith. The believer resists — does not flee or surrender. The resistance is in the faith — grounded in the truths of who Christ is and who the believer is in Him.

The Armor of God

Ephesians 6:10-11 — Geneva 1599:

"Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that ye may be able to stand against the assaults of the devil..."

The full armor:

  • Belt of truth (v. 14).
  • Breastplate of righteousness (v. 14).
  • Feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace (v. 15).
  • Shield of faith (v. 16).
  • Helmet of salvation (v. 17).
  • Sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (v. 17).
  • All prayer and supplication in the Spirit (v. 18).

The believer is to put on the full armor and stand.

Resisting Temptation

James 4:7 — Geneva 1599:

"Submit yourselves to God: resist the devil, and he will flee from you."

Two commands in order:

  1. Submit to God.
  2. Resist the devil.

The order matters. Submission to God is the foundation; resistance to the devil is the result. The believer who submits to God can resist the devil; the devil will flee.

1 Corinthians 10:13 — Geneva 1599:

There hath no temptation taken you, but such as appertain (applies) to man: and God is faithful, which will not suffer you to be tempted above that you be able, but will even give the issue with the temptation, that ye may be able to bear it.

Observations

(1) Temptation is common to humanity — no temptation is unique or unprecedented.

(2) God is faithful — He will not allow temptation beyond your ability to bear.

(3) He provides the way of escape — "ἔκβασις" — the exit. With every temptation, the Father provides a way out, that the believer may be able to bear it.

The believer's responsibility is to look for the way of escape and take it.

Practical Implications

1. Be alert. Recognize you are in conflict. The devil seeks to devour. Be watchful.

2. Put on the armor daily. Through prayer, Scripture, and conscious dependence on the Lord, equip yourself for battle.

3. Flee youthful lusts (2 Tim 2:22). Some temptations are to be resisted; others are to be fled. Sexual temptation, especially, is to be fled. Joseph fled Potiphar's wife (Gen 39:12). The believer does not stay to debate temptation; he flees.

4. Look for the way of escape. When temptation comes, ask: "Father, show me the way of escape." And then take it.

5. Submit before resisting. Submission to God precedes resistance to the devil.

6. Be especially watchful in seasons of weakness — fatigue, hunger, isolation, success (which can produce pride), failure (which can produce despair).

7. Have accountability partners. Other believers who will ask hard questions and pray with you in your struggles.

PART 7 — CONFESSION OF SIN

The believer is not sinless. Failure occurs. The discipline of confession is the means by which fellowship with the Father is maintained.

The Foundation: 1 John 1:9

1 John 1:9 — Geneva 1599:

"If we acknowledge our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

Observations

(1) ὁμολογῶμεν — "confess" — literally "to say the same thing" (ὁμό + λέγω). To confess sin is to agree with God about it — naming it for what He calls it, not minimizing or excusing.

(2) The promise is twofold:

  • ἀφῇ — forgive — the legal release from the debt of sin.
  • καθαρίσῃ — cleanse — the removal of the stain from the conscience and life.

(3) The basis — "He is faithful and just." Forgiveness is not because God is sentimental or lenient, but because He is faithful to His promise and just toward the propitiation Christ made.

The Distinction: Position vs. Fellowship

A vital theological distinction must be held:

Positionally, the believer's sins — past, present, and future — were dealt with at the cross. He is forgiven, justified, accepted in the Beloved. This is not undone by daily sin.

Practically (in fellowship), daily sin grieves the indwelling Spirit (Eph 4:30) and disrupts the believer's experiential communion with the Father. Confession restores the experiential fellowship.

1 John 1:9 addresses the practical/fellowship dimension — the believer's daily walk, his conscience, his communion. The position is secure; the fellowship requires confession.

The Pattern of Daily Confession

The believer should make confession a daily, regular practice:

  1. At the close of the day — review the day before the Lord, confessing known sin.
  2. At the moment of conviction — when the Spirit convicts of specific sin, confess immediately.
  3. Before the Lord's Supper — self-examination per 1 Cor 11.
  4. Before significant prayer — clearing the channels.

Confession to Other Believers

James 5:16 — Geneva 1599:

"Acknowledge your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed: for the prayer of a righteous man availeth much, if it be fervent."

Observation

Some sins should be confessed to other trusted believers — for prayer, accountability, and healing. This is not the priestly confessional of Rome (per maxim #3), but the genuine confession of brethren to one another for mutual support.

This is particularly helpful for besetting sins, sins of pride that need to be exposed in humility, or sins against specific persons that require their forgiveness.

Practical Implications

1. Confess sin promptly — do not let unconfessed sin accumulate.

2. Be specific in confession — name the sin clearly, not in vague generalities.

3. Receive forgiveness by faith — believe the promise of 1 John 1:9. Do not wallow in self-condemnation after God has forgiven.

4. Make restitution where required — confession may need to be accompanied by reconciliation with those wronged.

5. Confess corporate sin — sometimes the believer confesses on behalf of his nation, family, or community (as Daniel did in Dan 9).

6. Do not let the enemy use confession against you — once forgiven, you are forgiven. The accuser will try to bring back what God has remembered no more.

PART 8 — THE BELIEVER'S RESPONSE TO TRIALS

The believer encounters varied trials. The Christian's response is distinct from the world's.

The General Pattern: Joy in Trial

James 1:2-4 — Geneva 1599:

"My brethren, count it exceeding joy, when ye fall into divers temptations, Knowing that the trying of your faith bringeth forth patience, And let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, lacking nothing."

Observations

(1) Count it all joy — not because trials are pleasant, but because of what they accomplish.

(2) Trials produce ὑπομονή — patience, endurance, steadfast perseverance. The believer's character is forged through trial.

(3) Patience produces maturity — "perfect and entire, lacking nothing."

The believer's response: joy, because the Father is using the trial for His perfecting work.

The Different Kinds of Trials

Persecution for Righteousness

We examined this fully in our earlier discussion of suffering with Christ. The response: rejoice (Matt 5:11-12), bless (Rom 12:14), count it joy to be counted worthy to suffer for the Name (Acts 5:41).

Affliction in the Body

Illness, weakness, pain, the limitations of mortal life. The response: trust the Father's purpose, seek prayer (James 5:14-16), submit to the Father's wisdom, endure with hope of the resurrection (Rom 8:23).

Loss and Bereavement

The death of loved ones, the loss of relationships, the breaking of dear things. The response: grieve, but not as those without hope (1 Thess 4:13). Christian grief is real; it is also held within the certainty of resurrection.

Economic Hardship

Job loss, financial pressure, poverty. The response: trust the Father's provision (Matt 6:25-34), work diligently (2 Thess 3:10-12), be content (Phil 4:11-13), seek the kingdom first (Matt 6:33).

Relational Trials

Conflict, betrayal, loneliness, marital difficulty. The response: pray for those who hurt you (Matt 5:44), forgive as Christ forgave (Col 3:13), seek peace as far as it depends on you (Rom 12:18), trust the Lord for outcomes you cannot control.

Inner Trials

Depression, anxiety, doubt, dryness in prayer. The response: bring it honestly before the Lord (the Psalms model this), rest in His unchanging promises even when feelings vary, seek the help of trusted brethren, be patient with the slow work of the Spirit in dark seasons.

Temptation

Already discussed. The response: flee or resist as appropriate; look for the way of escape.

The Sustaining Truths

In every trial, the believer holds fast to certain truths:

  1. The Father is sovereign — nothing reaches you outside His permission.
  2. The Father is loving — He does not afflict from caprice or cruelty.
  3. All things work for good (Rom 8:28) — even this.
  4. Christ has been there — He sympathizes with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15).
  5. The Spirit indwells — strengthening, comforting, interceding.
  6. The trial is temporary — "light affliction which is but for a moment" (2 Cor 4:17).
  7. The glory is coming — incomparably greater than the present sufferings (Rom 8:18).
  8. Nothing separates us from His love (Rom 8:38-39).

Practical Implications

1. Do not be surprised by trials (1 Pet 4:12). They are normal in the Christian life.

2. Bring trials to the Father in prayer. Do not bear them alone.

3. Look for the lessons the Father is teaching. What patience is He growing? What dependence? What conformity to the Son?

4. Seek the help of the Body. Bear one another's burdens.

5. Use the trial as an opportunity to witness. Many have come to faith through observing Christians under trial.

6. Keep eternal perspective. This life is not the end of the story.

7. Be honest with God in your grief. The Psalms model this. You do not have to pretend.

PART 9 — WITNESS AND PROCLAMATION

The believer is called to bear witness to the Son before the world.

The Mandate

Matthew 28:19-20 — Geneva 1599:

"Go therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the Name of the Father, and the Son, and the holy Ghost, Teaching them to observe all things, whatsoever I have commanded you: and lo, I am with you alway, until the end of the world, Amen."

The Great Commission belongs to every believer, in its various spheres of application.

The Posture of the Witness

1 Peter 3:15 — Geneva 1599:

"But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you, with meekness and reverence,"

Observations

(1) Sanctify the Lord in your hearts — give Him the place of supremacy first internally. This is the foundation of all witness.

(2) Be ready — be prepared to give an answer. The believer should know the Gospel well enough to articulate it.

(3) For the hope that is in you — the witness centers on the hope — the certain expectation of glory through Christ.

(4) With meekness and reverence — not arrogantly, not combatively. The witness is winsome, humble, reverent.

The Believer's Witness

The believer witnesses in multiple ways:

By Life

Matthew 5:16 — Geneva 1599:

"Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."

The believer's life — his integrity, his love, his joy in trial, his honesty, his faithfulness — is itself a witness to the world.

By Word

Romans 10:14-15 — Geneva 1599:

"But how shall they call on him, in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him, of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them which bring glad tidings of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

Faith comes by hearing (Rom 10:17). The Gospel must be proclaimed verbally. Lives alone are insufficient — the explicit Gospel must be spoken.

By Service

Acts of mercy, compassion, and service open doors for the Gospel and embody it visibly.

The Content of the Witness

The Gospel itself — the good news that:

  • The Father loved the world and sent His Beloved Son.
  • The Son died for our sins and rose again the third day.
  • He is now at the Father's right hand, the appointed Lord and Christ.
  • Whoever believes in Him receives forgiveness and eternal life.
  • He will return to judge the living and the dead.
  • All who are in Him are children of God, indwelt by the Spirit, destined for glory.

This is the core. The believer should know how to articulate it briefly and clearly.

Practical Implications

1. Live a life consistent with your message. Hypocrisy nullifies witness.

2. Be ready to speak when opportunities arise. Pray for opportunities; recognize them; take them.

3. Be honest about your own journey. Personal testimony is powerful — "I was blind, now I see" (John 9:25).

4. Be patient with the lost. Conversion is the Father's work; you are a faithful witness.

5. Pray for the lost. Especially those near to you — family, neighbors, coworkers.

6. Support the proclamation of the Gospel — pray for and give to those engaged in missions and evangelism beyond your immediate reach.

7. Do not be ashamed of the Gospel (Rom 1:16). It is the power of God unto salvation.

PART 10 — STEWARDSHIP

The believer recognizes that nothing is truly his own — all has been entrusted by the Father for His purposes.

The Foundation

1 Corinthians 4:7

"For who separateth thee? and what hast thou, that thou hast not received? if thou hast received it, why rejoicest thou, as though thou hadst not received it?"

The believer has received everything he has. He is not an owner but a steward.

Time Stewardship

Ephesians 5:15-17

"Take heed therefore that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the season: for the days are evil. Wherefore, be ye not unwise, but understand what the will of the Lord is."

The believer is to redeem the time (ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν — "buying up the opportunity"). Time is finite and irretrievable; the believer uses it wisely for the Father's purposes.

Material Stewardship

1 Timothy 6:17-19

"Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not high-minded, and that they trust not in uncertain riches, but in the living God, (which giveth us abundantly, all things to enjoy) That they do good, and be rich in good works, and ready to distribute, and communicate (share), Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may obtain eternal life."

The believer with material resources:

  • Does not put trust in riches.
  • Does good with his resources.
  • Is ready to distribute.
  • Is generous, willing to share.

2 Corinthians 9:6-8

"This yet remember, that he which soweth sparingly, shall reap also sparingly, and he that soweth liberally, shall reap also liberally. As every man wisheth in his heart, so let him give, not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. And God is able to make all grace to abound toward you, that ye always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound in every good work,"

Giving is to be:

  • Decided in advance (as one purposes in his heart).
  • Cheerful (not grudging).
  • Generous (he who sows sparingly reaps sparingly).
  • Trusting (God is able to make all grace abound).

Stewardship of Gifts

1 Peter 4:10
